title: Trip & Surge Pricing
description: Design trip state machines, dynamic surge pricing based on supply-demand ratio, geohash-partitioned dispatch, and ETA computation with live traffic data.

segments.text: Every ride follows a state machine: requested, matched, driver_en_route, arrived, in_trip, completed, or cancelled. Each transition has rules — you can't go from requested to in_trip without matching. At Uber, the trip state machine is the central source of truth, and every downstream system — billing, driver pay, analytics — reacts to state transitions.

State transitions must be atomic and idempotent. Two concurrent 'cancel' requests shouldn't double-refund. Use optimistic locking with version numbers — read the trip with version five, update to cancelled only if version is still five. If another update happened first, retry. This prevents race conditions in the most critical business logic.

Surge pricing — Uber calls it dynamic pricing — adjusts prices based on the supply-demand ratio in a geographic area. If there are one hundred riders and twenty drivers, the surge multiplier might be two point five times. The goal: incentivize more drivers to come online and reduce demand to match available supply. Economics, not engineering, is the primary driver.

Surge is computed per geohash cell, updated every thirty seconds. Count active riders requesting in each cell, count available drivers. Compute the ratio. Apply a pricing curve — below one point two ratio, no surge. Above two, surge climbs aggressively. Smooth between adjacent cells to prevent price cliffs — a rider walking one block shouldn't see three times the price.

There's a concert ending and twenty thousand people need rides simultaneously in a four-block area. Your surge algorithm computes ten times pricing. But this causes public outrage and regulatory scrutiny. How do you balance market economics with fairness?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you cap surge pricing during predictable high-demand events while still incentivizing driver supply?

segments.text: The dispatch system is partitioned by geohash to enable horizontal scaling. Each partition handles matching for its geographic area. A dispatch server for Manhattan doesn't need to know about drivers in Brooklyn. Cross-partition matching happens at boundaries — a rider at the edge of two partitions might match with a driver in either partition.

ETA computation uses live traffic data from driver GPS traces. Uber collects billions of GPS points daily to build a real-time traffic graph. Road segments are weighted by current travel speed. Dijkstra's algorithm finds the fastest route, not shortest. The model accounts for traffic signals, turn penalties, and one-way streets. ETAs are accurate to within two minutes ninety percent of the time.

Trip pricing combines base fare, per-minute rate, per-mile rate, and surge multiplier. The price is locked at request time — shown to the rider before confirming. This upfront pricing protects riders from unexpected charges and protects drivers from intentionally slow routes. Uber stores the price promise and reconciles against actual trip data.

Edge cases in trip management: driver cancels after arriving — rider gets rematched with priority. Rider's phone dies mid-trip — the trip continues using driver's GPS, billing completes. Route mismatch — actual route differs from quoted route by twenty percent — automatic fare adjustment. Each edge case needs explicit handling in the state machine.

Design the trip and pricing system for a ride-sharing platform operating in fifty cities with different regulatory requirements — some cities ban surge pricing, some require fare caps. How do you make the system configurable per city?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a trip + pricing system configurable per city with different regulatory constraints.

segments.text: Trip management is a state machine with atomic transitions and optimistic locking. Surge pricing balances supply and demand per geohash cell with smoothing. ETA uses live traffic-weighted routing graphs. The Staff-level insight: ride-sharing is as much a marketplace design problem as a technical one — pricing affects supply, which affects matching, which affects rider experience.
